current_description.description_long: A New York Times report published May 20, 1981, said more than 50 well-known conservatives had convened the Council for National Policy, a new umbrella group they hoped would gain influence. Decades later, the TrumpFile page linked in this record describes a compilation of 1,011 names covering 1981 through 2020 and cautions that it may include fewer than half of the council’s members. Documented published a separate leaked September 2020 membership directory naming 426 people. Those figures describe different lists and should not be combined into a count of total members. Neither the linked compilation nor the supplied material verifies Donald Trump’s membership, position or participation in a CNP activity, and a person’s appearance in a multi-decade list would not by itself prove a role in a specific policy. The supported subject is the council’s formation and the scope and limitations of publicly available membership lists. Unless a reliable record connects Trump to the organization, this should be reframed as CNP history or excluded from a Trump-specific claim.

identified_problems.explanation: No credible primary record or reputable contemporaneous reporting reviewed substantiated the alleged $100,000 fee-for-access scheme or the claimed formal Office of Government Ethics complaint.

claims.claim: Melania Trump's office offered White House meetings for fees starting around $100,000 in 2025.
A formal Office of Government Ethics complaint was filed over the arrangement.
claims.notes: No complaint matching the allegation was located.

frozen_original.title: Melania Trump Charges $100,000 for White House Meetings, Ethics Complaint Filed
frozen_original.synopsis: Reports emerged in 2025 that Melania Trump's office was offering access to White House meetings with the First Lady for fees reportedly starting around $100,000, with the arrangement channeled through her personal business ventures. Ethics watchdogs filed formal complaints with the Office of Government Ethics arguing the arrangements violated federal ethics laws prohibiting the use of public office for private gain. Critics drew contrasts with previous first ladies who maintained non-commercial public roles. The revelations came against a backdrop of extensive Trump family monetization of the presidency, including the $TRUMP and $MELANIA memecoins, Mar-a-Lago foreign government access, and Kushner's foreign investment deals. The administration declined to comment on the specific arrangements.

proposal.original_claim_summary: Vought Acting CFPB Director Shuts Down Bureau and Fires Entire Staff
proposal.original_synopsis: Russell Vought, while simultaneously serving as OMB Director, was appointed acting director of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and immediately shut down the agency, halting all pending cases against financial predators and firing virtually all of its 1,700 employees. The CFPB was created after the 2008 financial crisis specifically to protect consumers from predatory lending, bank fraud, and deceptive financial products. Its shutdown eliminated the primary federal agency protecting ordinary Americans from financial exploitation, benefiting the financial industry donors who had funded Trump's campaigns.

frozen_original.title: Trump Reveals Golf Course Plans to Japanese PM Abe at Mar-a-Lago
frozen_original.synopsis: During Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe's visit to Mar-a-Lago on February 10-11, 2017, Trump used the occasion—billed as a summit on North Korea, trade, and bilateral relations—to discuss his private golf course business with Abe. Japanese media reported that Trump showed Abe plans for a potential Trump-brand golf course in Japan, blurring the line between presidential diplomacy and personal business promotion. The visit to Mar-a-Lago itself—where non-member guests could witness the two leaders' dinner and discussions in the semi-public dining room—drew scrutiny about security protocols and the use of a private club as an impromptu diplomatic venue. Ethics experts noted that using presidential meetings to advance personal business interests represented an unprecedented breach of the separation between the office and private gain.
